$comment: An EXAMPLE rule set for the merge-triage task. Copy it into your repo and rewrite it; do not depend
on this file. Rule sets encode what a specific repo guarantees, which is the one part that must never
be generic, so they live in the consuming repo rather than here.
Two things that matter more than the patterns:
- `why` is read by a human under time pressure. It should say what to check and what breaks if it
is wrong. A rule whose `why` restates the file name is worse than no rule, because it adds noise
to a report people are meant to trust.
- Order carries meaning: first match wins, so specific rules go above general ones.

rules.why: Authorisation. Check whether a permission check gained or lost a caller, and whether a new code path reaches data without passing one.
A migration. Check whether it drops or re-predicates an index your queries depend on: that degrades every query using it without failing a single test.
The API surface changed. A new read endpoint is a new way to reach data; confirm it is covered by whatever asserts your access rules.
A data-access layer. Check whether a query that returns records gained or lost a filter, and whether an existing filter is still attached to the query it was written for.
Business logic. Usually benign, but this is where a read path can quietly start returning more than it used to.
